title: Vayetze: angels at the border (Genesis 32:2–3)
hook: the portion opens and closes with angels at the edges of the journey

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stone meant for many, moved by one man in love. Your line was love moves stones. Today, twenty years later, Jacob heads home.

A first day at a new job. The drive home from the hospital with a newborn. The last box carried out of an apartment. Some days are thresholds, the strip at the foot of a doorway, and they don't run like ordinary days. Jacob arrived in Haran with a staff. Twenty years later, he leaves with two wives, Leah and Rachel, eleven sons and a daughter, flocks, servants, and a complicated relationship with his father-in-law, Laban. Laban chases him, they argue, they make a covenant, and they part. Jacob is finally going home.
screen: `THRESHOLDS FEEL DIFFERENT.` → `TWENTY YEARS IN HARAN.` → `JACOB HEADS HOME.`

segments.voice: This portion is built like a pair of bookends. It opened with Jacob leaving home, sleeping on a stone, dreaming of angels going up and down a ladder. And it closes, twenty years later, like this, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him." He sees them and says, this is God's camp, and he names the place Mahanaim, which means two camps. Angels at the start of the journey, angels at the end, and in between a whole life: marriages, children, hard work, being cheated, and learning to hold his own. The rabbis noticed the bookends and asked what they meant. Rashi, back at the ladder, has a striking picture. Why do the angels go up first and then come down? Because the angels who had been with Jacob in the land of Israel went up at the border, and a new group of angels came down to go with him outside it. A changing of the guard. And here at Mahanaim, Rashi says the same thing happens in reverse: the angels who went with him abroad and the angels of the land meet at the border, to hand him over. Two camps, one traveler. The Torah itself only tells us angels met him; it doesn't say what they did or said. But Rashi's picture is easy to carry: Jacob doesn't cross that border alone. At the edge, one company lets go of him, and another is waiting.
screen: `ANGELS AT THE LADDER.` · `TWENTY YEARS IN BETWEEN.` · `ANGELS OF GOD MET HIM.` · `MAHANAIM: TWO CAMPS.` · then, large: `ANGELS AT EVERY BORDER.`

segments.voice: Think of what's starting or finishing in your life right now: a new job, a child leaving, a friendship changing, the end of a season. Picture yourself standing at that border, and notice who is letting go of you on one side and who is waiting on the other. Maybe a person; maybe, if you believe it, something more.
Vayetze. And he went out: the portion that opens and closes with angels, at the edges of Jacob's twenty-year journey.
Your line: angels at every border. At the ladder, and again at Mahanaim. That's day one hundred ninety-five.
